chapter_theme: Giving: give gladly and daily within one's means, even when poor and even a grain's worth, to those who cannot repay, because death and age are near and wealth comes and goes by past merit, not by clutching. The fame of giving outlasts all else, and one who cannot give should at least not beg.
structure_note: The reasons offered shift through the chapter: the next world (91, 94, 95), impermanence (92), merit governing wealth (93), the good of the world (96, 97), the nature of a true gift (98, 99) and fame (100).

91.reading: Those whose nature is to give gladly, as much as they can, even when they have little, as if they had plenty, will not find the doors of that world shut against them.
91.nuance: Gladness is part of the qualification: the gift is measured against the giver's means and his spirit, not its size.

positions.position: The doors are those of the other world, which Pope calls heaven.
The doors are those of release (வீடுபேறு), not of a heaven.

92.reading: Death's day and hateful old age stand right before you, and disease that destroys strength comes after; don't run about in vain, don't clutch, share before you eat, and hide nothing while wealth is in your hand.
92.nuance: The case for giving here is impermanence, not merit or fame: wealth is to be used while the hand still holds it. Mudaliar takes பரவன்மின் as 'don't roam after more wealth'; Pope has 'indulge not discursive thoughts'.

93.reading: Whether one ignores the misery of those who come trembling or gives and enjoys, wealth gathers when its time to gather comes; and however tightly it is held, it leaves when the good deeds that sent it run out.
93.nuance: The argument removes the miser's motive: giving can't lose wealth that merit holds, and clutching can't keep wealth that merit has stopped holding. Mudaliar notes the variant இடுக்குற்று (clutching tight) for மிடுக்குற்று (with force).

94.reading: Give daily, before eating, from what you can, even a grain of rice's worth; the quatrain backs this with a saying about those who do not give and those whose hearth is never lit.

positions.position: உம்மை means 'in a former birth': those who did not give then are the poor with unlit hearths now.
உம்மை means 'you': the poor with unlit hearths will scorn you as misers.
positions.quote: கொடாத கருமிகள் என்று உம்மை இழித்து உரைப்பர்.

95.reading: With an eye to the next world and this one, give what you can in a fitting way; and if poverty makes giving impossible, not begging is worth twice as much as giving.
95.nuance: Mudaliar names the two rewards: heavenly joy in the next world and renown in this one. The last line keeps the poor inside the economy of giving: they give by not taking.

96.reading: Those who live so that many desire them are like a fruit-bearing palm enclosed by a platform in the middle of town; those who do not give before eating, even when their household thrives, are like a barren male palm in the burning ground.
96.nuance: Both are palms; fruit and place separate them. The giver stands where everyone gathers, the miser among the dead.

97.reading: Lord of the cool shore of the pounding sea, where the punnai's scent drives off the smell of fish: if the rain does not fall when it should, and the world does not do what it should, how will the world survive?
97.nuance: Both commentators take the 'world' that must act to be its good or wise people, so their giving is set beside rain as a second support of life.

98.reading: Never refusing an outstretched hand and holding nothing back, to give to those who can't repay is a man's duty; lord of the cool shore, giving to those who will give back earns only the name of a profitable loan.
98.nuance: Mudaliar lists several ways to take தாம் வரையாது: excluding no gift, excluding no person, setting no rules, or keeping nothing back for oneself.

99.reading: Never say 'it is too little' or 'I have nothing'; always do the good of giving, to anyone, for like the ascetic's bowl filled at door after door, it fills slowly.
99.nuance: The bowl belongs to the one who receives, but it stands for what fills in the giver: Mudaliar says the fruit of virtue fills his life, Shanmuganar that good deeds accumulate.

100.reading: A drum struck with a stick is heard a காதம் away and rolling thunder a யோசனை, but the word 'they gave', linked with the worthy, is heard through all three stacked worlds.
100.nuance: Mudaliar records a third reading, 'they gave to the worthy'.

positions.position: The word is 'he gave', spoken by the worthy about a giver.
The word is praise that the worthy themselves gave.

links.note: Both hold that giving does not wait for wealth: 218 says those who know their duty don't falter in helping even when means are gone, and 91 rewards those who give gladly when they have little.
Both argue from impermanence: 333 says wealth does not stay, so do what lasts at once, and 92 says death, age and disease are near, so share while wealth is in hand.

Both deny that guarding keeps wealth: 376 says what is not one's own won't stay however it is guarded, and 93 that wealth leaves when its merit runs out however tightly held. 376 names fate; 93 names past deeds.

Both explain the many poor by what was not done: 270 by the few who practise austerity, and 94 in Mudaliar's reading by the failure to give in a former birth. They give different causes for the same fact without denying each other.
Both put a number on not begging: 1061 says it is worth ten million times more even when givers are glad, and 95 that it is worth twice as much as giving.
Both put the giver's wealth in a fruiting tree at the town's centre, where all can reach it.
1008 keeps the tree in the town's centre but makes the miser's wealth a poison tree fruiting there; 96 moves the miser's barren palm out to the burning ground.
211 makes the rain the model of help that seeks no return. 97 sets rain and the good's giving side by side as the two things the world can't survive without.
In 19 giving depends on rain: if the sky fails, giving and austerity cease. In 97 the two are parallel supports, each needed on its own.
Both say giving to those who can repay is not giving but lending: 221 calls it a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை), and 98 a profitable loan (பொலிகடன்).
Both turn on small things adding up: in 475 peacock feathers, piled high enough, break a cart's axle, and in 99 small gifts fill the bowl. One warns, the other encourages.
Both make giving the source of lasting praise: 232 says all that speakers praise rests on those who give to the asker, and 100 that the word 'they gave' is heard through three worlds.

source_issues: 92: Shanmuganar's field also contains the Tamil of 93 (reading தாந் துய்ப்பினும் and இடுக்குற்று) and his commentary on it.
93: Shanmuganar's commentary is not aligned (it sits at the end of 92's field).
